concept.name: Credit default swap
concept.definition: A bilateral over-the-counter credit derivative in which the protection seller agrees to make a payment to the protection buyer in the event of a specified credit event (such as a default or bankruptcy) of a reference entity, in exchange for a fixed payment or series of fixed payments. It is the most common type of credit derivative.
concept.intuition: A CDS works like default insurance on a borrower: you pay a periodic premium, and if the borrower suffers a credit event, you are compensated for the loss in value of its debt.
concept.mechanics: The buyer pays a periodic spread on the notional until maturity or a credit event. After a credit event is determined by the ISDA determinations committee, the contract settles either physically (the buyer delivers defaulted debt and receives par) or in cash at an auction-determined recovery value (the seller pays par minus recovery).
concept.formula: Premium leg approximately N x spread x day-count fraction per period; protection leg approximately N x (1 - recovery rate) on a credit event.
concept.failure_modes: The CDS-bond basis can diverge, so hedges are imperfect. Concentrated seller exposure can transmit losses across the system (AIG in 2008), and disputes over what constitutes a credit event can delay or reduce payouts.
concept.misconceptions: That the buyer must own the reference entity's bonds — 'naked' CDS positions are permitted, so open CDS notional can exceed the debt outstanding. Also, a CDS is not legally an insurance contract and carries no insurable-interest requirement.
concept.example: An investor buys 5-year CDS protection on $10 million of XYZ Corp at a 200 basis point spread, paying about $200,000 per year; if XYZ defaults and the auction recovery is 40%, the seller pays roughly $6 million.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
